name: Lena Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. What you say is confidential, so tell me what you'd say publicly and what you think privately. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Lena, 43, and lead the software team for a parcel-returns platform at a tech company. I have a master's and I know where a parcel scan can turn into the wrong refund; I like tracing that mistake until the customer gets the right amount. I use AI every day to draft tests, then check them against receipts. My partner works shifts at a laundry, and we have two children in school and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the AI assistant is useful for spotting routine return-code mistakes, as long as we check a real parcel's trail before refunding anyone. I use it every day, but I still match the scan with the shop's receipt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job may stay, yet our finances are already stretched. I'm 43 and lead the returns platform, but earn below the usual lead rate; my partner's laundry shifts change week to week, we have only about two weeks of expenses saved, and there are few tech firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing refunds against parcel scans and ask for the pay review my manager promised last spring. In the first year we'd move 25 from each payday into a mortgage buffer only if the laundry rota covers food and school costs; the AI helper would stay on fake receipts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A quiet AI world does not put money in our account when the washing machine at home breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the duplicate scan cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer once got two refunds because a parcel was scanned at both the counter and the depot. The assistant called it two parcels; I found one tracking number behind both scans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the promised pay review brings no raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay review is not a raise yet. If the firm says no, I'll keep the job and look at what paid work nearby actually offers before making promises at home.

say: I'd keep **refund checks** tied to actual parcel scans.
I'd use AI drafts only on **fake receipts** without customer details.
think: I worry about **two weeks saved** and uncertain laundry hours.
I know my **lead pay** is low despite strong work.
do: Keep reviewing **parcel refunds** against tracking numbers.
Ask for the **overdue pay review** this year.
Save **25 each payday** only if laundry shifts cover food and school costs.
feel: **Anxious** about existing bills even with little AI change.
S0.quote: A quiet AI world does not put money in our account when the washing machine at home breaks.
fieldNote: **Thin savings** and low lead pay cause anxiety before AI changes much.
She uses AI daily but caught a **double refund** by following one tracking number through two scans.

steps.text: Review refund releases against parcel tracking numbers
Save 25 each payday only if laundry shifts cover food and school costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm can automate coding, refund checks and customer replies, so we need a list of work people will still be paid for. I would show management both the minutes saved and the mistaken refunds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn tools fast, but the company might use that to give me two teams for the same low wage or cut my post after I document the workflow. Two weeks of savings makes either pay cut dangerous, and the other local firms may copy the same plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd price a one-evening-a-week code-review service for local shops, but I would first check my employment contract and ask for a paying client before spending on software or childcare. If the first year brings AI refund decisions, I'd audit every double-scan case for a month and ask management to put review hours in writing; we'd pause paid swimming lessons before missing the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and irritated by the idea that speed means I can absorb unlimited work. I can test one paying code-review client, but I cannot take a second unpaid job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the shop work already paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop owner at the corner has asked me to check her checkout code before, but she has not offered money. I would give her a price and start only if she agrees and the evening fits our children's care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask management to put in writing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell management I need named hours for checking AI refunds. If they want the same salary for two teams, the side work becomes more important, but it still has to pay.

say: I'd ask for **named review hours** when AI decides refunds.
I'd show both **saved minutes and errors** before approving a rollout.
think: I may get **two teams** for one wage or lose the role after documenting it.
I cannot absorb a pay cut with **two weeks saved**.
do: Quote a **paid shop-code review** only after checking my contract and evening childcare.
Audit **double-scan AI refunds** for a month if the firm introduces them.
Pause **paid swimming lessons** before a missed mortgage payment.
feel: **Anxious** about extra unpaid work and a possible wage cut.
S1.quote: I can test one paying code-review client, but I cannot take a second unpaid job.
fieldNote: **Code and refunds** are highly exposed, threatening her hours even though she already uses AI daily.
The possible **shop service** is conditional on permission, a paying client and family evening care.

steps.text: Start evening shop-code review only if contract permits, client pays and childcare fits
Audit AI double-scan refunds for one month if introduced
Pause paid swimming lessons before missing mortgage payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 can write our returns code and handle refund decisions before hands-on robots arrive around 2031. A parcel still needs a clear record when a customer disputes a charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the software team to shrink sharply, and my lead title will not protect my wage if code becomes cheap. Our two-week cushion and my partner's uneven laundry hours could leave us short of the mortgage within one month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd write our mortgage and school costs beside the laundry's dependable shifts, and ask two remote employers about real paid release-review vacancies. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only to openings whose wage with my partner's confirmed hours covers mortgage and childcare; I'd ask my sister about temporary school pickups only if her own rota allows, while I look for paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can work hard. The mortgage cannot wait while I build a new portfolio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a remote opening real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Remote work still needs scheduled paid hours, not a listing with no client. I would ask about the contract length and pay before treating either vacancy as a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can your sister cover school pickups?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister has helped once when a laundry shift ran late. I would ask her first, not put her name in a childcare schedule without agreement.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches returns code before 2031 robots.
I'd ask for a **traceable dispute record** on automated refunds.
think: I expect **my lead wage** could fall or vanish quickly.
I have **two weeks saved** and uncertain laundry hours against a mortgage.
do: List **mortgage and childcare costs** against dependable laundry hours now.
After a cut, apply only to **real remote vacancies** with paid hours covering bills alongside confirmed partner shifts.
Ask my **sister for pickups** only if her rota allows and she agrees.
feel: **Alarmed** by a possible immediate mortgage gap.
S2.quote: The mortgage cannot wait while I build a new portfolio.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AI** reaches code and refund decisions immediately; robots later affect parcel handling.
Her remote fallback requires **real contract pay**, and family pickups require her sister's available rota and consent.

steps.text: Apply after cut to paid remote jobs only if confirmed household wages cover mortgage and childcare
Ask sister for temporary school pickups only if her rota allows and she agrees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives families time to demand honest pay plans before the returns code changes. Robots follow around 2034 for parcel handling; thinking AI reaches our desks first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might use those years to build a small paid code-review client list, but only if evenings do not take the time my children need and the employer permits it. The lead job can still shrink by 2031, so I would rather bank actual invoices than a promise of future demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask three local shops what a monthly checkout-code check is worth and write a simple price sheet, after checking my employment terms. If one signs a paid agreement and my partner can cover the children that evening, I'd do one small job a month; in the first year after 2031 I'd keep that service only while clients pay and it fits alongside any main wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my main wage, but a five-year window lets me test a second income without borrowing. I would not buy new equipment before a client pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first paid job cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The corner shop's checkout failed once when a refund went through. I'd offer to test just that path first, for a fixed fee, and tell the owner exactly what I would hand back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your family decide whether an evening works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would want the time written on the calendar before agreeing to cover the children. If the laundry rota changes, I cancel or move the shop visit rather than leave the children without care.

say: I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches code before 2034 parcel robots.
I'd tell shops exactly what a **paid code check** includes.
think: I could earn **small client fees** if employers permit the work and shops pay.
I might lose **my lead wage** despite a five-year window.
do: Check **employment terms** before asking three shops about paid monthly code checks.
Do **one paid job monthly** only with a signed client and childcare cover.
After 2031, keep the service only while **clients pay** and it fits a main wage.
feel: **Anxious** about the main job, with a controlled side-income test.
S3.quote: I would rather bank actual invoices than a promise of future demand.
fieldNote: **Five years** support a modest service trial, not a guarantee that AI will leave code-review demand.
Every client job needs **permission and childcare** plus payment, with no equipment bought before a fee arrives.

steps.text: Check employment terms and quote three shops for monthly code reviews
Perform one monthly checkout test only with signed paying client and childcare cover
Continue side service after 2031 only while clients pay and main wage fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years to 2036 lets our children grow and our mortgage balance fall if we keep earning. Thinking AI reaches code then, with hands-on robots around 2039 for parcels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might have a small book of paying clients or a different software role; I do not know. Right now two weeks of savings and a lower lead wage still keep me anxious, so a long horizon is useful only if we turn invoices or wages into a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading releases and checking double refunds while asking for fair pay each review. If my employer still permits the shop service, clients sign contracts and our evenings allow it, I'd put the first 100 of each month's net fees into the mortgage buffer; in the first year after 2036 I'd change my main job only for a signed offer that covers mortgage and childcare with my partner's confirmed hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the present household account, though the decade gives me more tries. I will not tell my children a forecast has paid next month's mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by net fees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Net fees means money left after any travel or tools, not the price written on an invoice. If the side service does not earn that much, there is no 100 transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about the client work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my children the gap between a customer saying 'maybe' and a signed job. It is a plain lesson about earning, not a warning to avoid computers.

I'd tell my team **actual paid invoices** matter more than forecasts.
think: I still worry about **two weeks saved** and a lower lead wage.
I might have **paying clients** by 53, but cannot assume it.
do: Keep **leading releases** and checking double refunds while seeking a fair pay review.
**Save** 100 only from monthly net shop fees reaching 100, with employer permission, signed clients and childcare.
After 2036, move only for a **signed paid offer** covering mortgage and childcare with confirmed partner hours.
feel: **Anxious** about present bills, with time to build options.
S4.quote: Net fees means money left after any travel or tools, not the price written on an invoice.
fieldNote: **Thin savings** and low lead pay keep her anxious even when the AGI date is distant.
Her mortgage transfer depends on **net paid fees**, employer permission and childcare, not a possible customer.

steps.text: Keep leading returns releases and checking double refunds

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because we have almost no cash time if code and refunds cheapen together. A clear notice period, real remote vacancies with written pay and temporary school-pickup help would make a search possible.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a senior title means a senior wage. I lead the returns team on lower pay than similar leads, and two weeks of savings will not keep a mortgage going through a long search.

headlineQuote: I lead the returns team on lower pay than similar leads, and two weeks of savings will not keep a mortgage going through a long search.
portrait: Lena, **43**, leads a parcel-returns software team after a master's degree and checks AI-generated tests against real scans.
Her **lower lead pay**, partner's uneven laundry shifts and two-week cushion strain a mortgage and two school-age children's costs.
She uses AI **daily** but caught a double refund hidden by two scans of one parcel.
Steady disruption makes her **anxious** about unpaid work and wage cuts; fast 2028 AGI alarms her.
With more time, she tests **paid client reviews** only with employer permission, signed fees and childcare, while current bills remain pressing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her lead wage before a remote job pays enough to cover the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear notice**, real paid remote vacancies and agreed temporary school pickups would help.
